title: A brainless slime mould recreated Tokyo's rail network in a dish

cover.alt: A bright yellow slime mould spread across a dark dish, with fan-shaped yellow fronts reaching out to pale flakes of food around it.

body: *Physarum polycephalum* is a single, huge cell with many nuclei, and it has no brain or nerves. As it spreads, it builds a web of tubes, then pulls back from the parts it does not need. In 2000 a Japanese and Hungarian team showed it could find the **shortest path through a maze** between two food sources. In a 2010 study, oat flakes laid out to stand for Tokyo and 36 surrounding towns ended up linked by tubes in a pattern similar to the real train system.

slides.alt: Time-lapse of a bright yellow slime mould spreading over a dark dish in fan-shaped fronts and covering the pale flakes of food around it, as the view pulls back.
slides.caption: Time-lapse: the slime mould Physarum polycephalum spreads across a dish in fan-shaped fronts and smothers the flakes of food around it.

slides.heading: How a single cell solves a maze

steps.label: It spreads into every corridor of the maze
It reaches oatmeal placed at two spots
It pulls back from every longer route
Only the shortest tube between foods is left

slides.label: top speed of the flow through its tubes
slides.text: Squeezes of the tube walls drive the flow. With enough food, the whole network-shaped cell can grow to a foot (30 cm) or more across.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: It is a kind of fungus
The whole yellow blob is one cell
It has a tiny, simple brain
It eats microbes such as bacteria

slides.explanation: It was long mistaken for a fungus, but it is an amoeba: one giant cell with many nuclei, no brain at all, that feeds on microbes.

slides.question: In the 2010 Tokyo experiment, what stood in for the city and its surrounding towns?
slides.explanation: Oat flakes marked Tokyo and 36 surrounding towns. The slime mould linked them with tubes in a network similar to the real rail system.
